questions.q: z₁ = 2(cos 40° + i sin 40°) and z₂ = 3(cos 20° + i sin 20°). What is z₁z₂ in the form a + bi?
questions.x: Multiply the moduli and add the arguments: z₁z₂ = 6(cos 60° + i sin 60°) = 6(½ + (√3/2)i) = 3 + 3√3 i. Adding the moduli instead gives 5/2 + (5√3/2)i; swapping cos and sin gives 3√3 + 3i.

questions.q: A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5}. What is the symmetric difference (A − B) ∪ (B − A)?
questions.x: A − B = {1, 2} and B − A = {5}, so their union is {1, 2, 5}. Check: it is A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} with A ∩ B = {3, 4} removed.

questions.q: At which points does the line y = x + 2 meet the parabola y = x²?
questions.x: x² = x + 2 gives x² − x − 2 = (x − 2)(x + 1) = 0, so x = 2 or x = −1, with y = 4 and y = 1. Both points satisfy both equations: 4 = 2 + 2 and 1 = −1 + 2.

questions.q: The point (2, 5) lies on the graph of a one-one function y = f(x). Which point must lie on the graph of y = f⁻¹(x)?
questions.x: f(2) = 5 means f⁻¹(5) = 2, so (5, 2) is on the graph of f⁻¹: the two graphs are mirror images in the line y = x. f⁻¹ is not 1/f, so (2, 1/5) is wrong.

questions.q: lim(x→2) f(x) = 5. What is lim(x→2) √(f(x) + 4)?
questions.x: By the limit theorems, lim √(f(x) + 4) = √(lim f(x) + 4) = √(5 + 4) = 3. The root of a sum is not the sum of the roots, so √5 + 2 is wrong.

questions.q: A 3 × 3 matrix A has |A| = 7. What is the rank of A?
questions.x: |A| ≠ 0, so A is non-singular and its echelon form has 3 non-zero rows: the rank is 3. The rank of a 3 × 3 matrix can never be more than 3, so 7 is impossible.

questions.q: Which value of x does NOT satisfy x² − 3x − 10 < 0?
questions.x: x² − 3x − 10 = (x − 5)(x + 2) < 0 for −2 < x < 5, with the end points excluded because the inequality is strict. At x = 5 the expression is 0, which is not less than 0. Check: 0, 4 and −1 give −10, −6 and −6.

questions.q: The parabola y = x² + bx + c has its vertex at (1, 4). What is the value of b + c?
questions.x: With vertex (1, 4), y = (x − 1)² + 4 = x² − 2x + 5, so b = −2, c = 5 and b + c = 3. Check: y(1) = 1 + b + c = 4 also gives b + c = 3 directly. Taking b = +2 gives 7.

questions.q: For some n, 1 + 2 + 3 + … + n = 55. What is 1³ + 2³ + 3³ + … + n³?
questions.x: Σk³ = [n(n + 1)/2]² = (Σk)², so it is 55² = 3025. Check: n(n + 1)/2 = 55 gives n = 10, and 10² × 11²/4 = 3025. 385 is the sum of squares for n = 10.

questions.q: What is the value of 1 × 10 + 2 × 9 + 3 × 8 + … + 10 × 1?
questions.x: The kth term is k(11 − k) = 11k − k², so the sum is 11 × 55 − 385 = 605 − 385 = 220. Check with n(n + 1)(n + 2)/6 for n = 10: 10 × 11 × 12/6 = 220. 385 is Σk² alone.

questions.q: In how many ways can 4 men and 4 women sit around a round table so that no two men sit next to each other?
questions.x: Seat the women first round the table: (4 − 1)! = 6 ways. This leaves 4 gaps between them, one man in each: 4! = 24 ways. Total 6 × 24 = 144. Treating the table as a row for the women (4! instead of 3!) gives 576.

questions.q: The period of a simple pendulum is T = 2π√(l/g). If the length l is increased by 2%, the period increases by approximately:
questions.x: The new period is 2π√(1.02 l/g) = T(1 + 0.02)^(1/2) ≈ T(1 + ½ × 0.02) = 1.01T, an increase of about 1%. Using the power 2 instead of ½ gives 4%.

questions.q: A wheel of radius 35 cm rolls 11 m along level ground without slipping. Through what angle does it turn? (Take π = 22/7.)
questions.x: The arc rolled out equals the distance: θ = 1100/35 = 220/7 rad. In degrees, 220/7 × 180/(22/7) = 1800°, which is 5 revolutions. Using the diameter instead of the radius gives 900°.

questions.q: Given tan θ = 1/2, what is tan 3θ?
For every x, 2 cos 5x sin x equals:
questions.x: 2 cos A sin B = sin(A + B) − sin(A − B); with A = 5x and B = x this is sin 6x − sin 4x. sin 6x + sin 4x is 2 sin 5x cos x, with the factors the other way round.

questions.q: The graph of y = cos x is symmetric about:
questions.x: cos(−x) = cos x, so cos is an even function and its graph is a mirror image in the y-axis. Symmetry about the origin belongs to odd functions such as sin x and tan x.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, a = 5, b = 6 and c = 7. What is cos A?
questions.x: cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc) = (36 + 49 − 25)/84 = 60/84 = 5/7. 19/35 is cos B and 1/5 is cos C, from putting the wrong side last.

questions.q: The range (principal values) of y = tan⁻¹x is:
questions.x: tan⁻¹x takes every value strictly between −π/2 and π/2; the end values are never reached because tan(±π/2) is undefined. [0, π] is the range of cos⁻¹x, and (0, π) that of cot⁻¹x.

questions.q: What is the derivative of y = (x + 1/x)², x ≠ 0?
questions.x: Expand: y = x² + 2 + 1/x², so y′ = 2x − 2/x³. Check by the chain rule: 2(x + 1/x)(1 − 1/x²) = 2(x − 1/x + 1/x − 1/x³) = 2x − 2/x³.

questions.q: The point (0, 1) lies on the curve eʸ + xy = e. What is dy/dx at this point?
questions.x: Differentiate: eʸ y′ + y + x y′ = 0. At (0, 1): e y′ + 1 = 0, so y′ = −1/e. Forgetting the product rule on xy (dropping the y term) would give 0, and inverting gives −e.

questions.q: If y = e^(x²), what is dy/dx at x = 1?
questions.x: dy/dx = e^(x²) × 2x by the chain rule, which is 2e at x = 1. Forgetting the factor 2x gives e.

questions.q: d/dx ∫ₓ¹ t² dt equals:
questions.x: ∫ₓ¹ t² dt = −∫₁ˣ t² dt, and by the Fundamental Theorem the derivative of ∫₁ˣ t² dt is x², so the answer is −x². Check: ∫ₓ¹ t² dt = 1/3 − x³/3, whose derivative is −x².

questions.q: ∫ dx/(x√(x² − 1)), for x > 1, equals:
questions.x: For x > 1, d/dx sec⁻¹x = 1/(x√(x² − 1)), so the antiderivative is sec⁻¹x + C. sin⁻¹x needs |x| < 1, and cosh⁻¹x has derivative 1/√(x² − 1), without the factor x.

questions.q: Which curve is the solution of x·y·dy/dx = 1 + y² with y = 0 when x = 1?
questions.x: Separate: y dy/(1 + y²) = dx/x, so ½ln(1 + y²) = ln x + c and 1 + y² = kx². y(1) = 0 gives k = 1, so y² = x² − 1. Check: 2yy′ = 2x, so xyy′ = x² = 1 + y².

questions.q: For what value of k does the line kx + 3y − 6 = 0 have its slope equal to its y-intercept?
questions.x: y = −(k/3)x + 2, so the slope is −k/3 and the y-intercept is 2. −k/3 = 2 gives k = −6.

questions.q: What is the area of the region x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, 2x + 3y ≤ 12?
questions.x: The region is the triangle with corners (0, 0), (6, 0) and (0, 4), so its area is ½ × 6 × 4 = 12. Forgetting the ½ gives 24.

questions.q: A dish has a parabolic cross-section y² = 4ax with its vertex at the origin. It is 40 cm across and 10 cm deep. How far from the vertex is the focus?
questions.x: A rim point is (10, 20): 400 = 40a, so a = 10 cm and the focus (a, 0) is 10 cm from the vertex. Using the full width 40 as y gives 1600 = 40a, i.e. 40 cm.

questions.q: A point P moves so that |PF₁ − PF₂| = 6, where F₁ = (−5, 0) and F₂ = (5, 0). What is the equation of its path?
questions.x: This is a hyperbola with 2a = 6 and c = 5, so a² = 9 and b² = 25 − 9 = 16: x²/9 − y²/16 = 1. Check the vertex (3, 0): |8 − 2| = 6.

questions.q: Forces F₁ = i + 2j + 3k and F₂ = 2i − j + k act together on a particle, which moves from A(0, 1, 2) to B(2, 3, 1). What is the total work done?
questions.x: Resultant F = 3i + j + 4k and displacement AB = 2i + 2j − k, so W = 6 + 2 − 4 = 4 units. Using F₁ alone gives 3.

questions.q: In the regula-falsi method on [a, b], where f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, the next approximation is where the chord through (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)) meets the x-axis. Which formula gives it?
questions.x: The chord meets y = 0 at x = a − f(a)(b − a)/(f(b) − f(a)) = (a·f(b) − b·f(a))/(f(b) − f(a)). Check with f(x) = x − 1 on [0, 2]: (0 − 2(−1))/(1 + 1) = 1, the root. (a + b)/2 is the bisection midpoint.

questions.q: Five readings of a time are 2.4 s, 2.6 s, 2.5 s, 2.7 s and 2.3 s. Taking the mean deviation as the uncertainty, rounded to one significant figure, the result is:
questions.x: Mean = 12.5/5 = 2.5 s. Deviations are 0.1, 0.1, 0, 0.2 and 0.2 s; their mean is 0.6/5 = 0.12 ≈ 0.1 s. Taking the largest deviation gives ± 0.2 s; the total of the deviations gives ± 0.6 s.

questions.q: A body is in equilibrium under the action of three coplanar forces that are not parallel. Their lines of action must:
o: Make equal angles of 120° with one another
questions.x: If two of the lines of action meet at a point, the third force must also pass through that point, or it would have a torque about it and the second condition would fail. Equal 120° angles apply only when the three forces are equal.

questions.q: A train slows uniformly from 30 m s⁻¹ to 10 m s⁻¹ over a distance of 200 m. The time this takes is:
questions.x: Average velocity = (30 + 10)/2 = 20 m s⁻¹, so t = 200/20 = 10 s. Check: a = (10² − 30²)/(2 × 200) = −2 m s⁻² and t = (10 − 30)/(−2) = 10 s. Dividing 200 m by the final speed gives 20 s.

questions.q: The velocity–time graph of a car is a straight line rising from 10 m s⁻¹ at t = 0 to 30 m s⁻¹ at t = 5 s. The distance covered in these 5 s is:
questions.x: Area of the trapezium = ½(10 + 30) × 5 = 100 m; check with s = ut + ½at², a = 4 m s⁻²: 50 + 50 = 100 m. Forgetting the ½ gives 200 m; using only the final speed gives 150 m.

questions.q: A 4 kg block slides on a rough horizontal floor against a constant friction force. Its speed falls from 6 m s⁻¹ to 4 m s⁻¹ while it slides 5 m. How much farther does it slide before stopping?
questions.x: Friction = loss of KE/distance = ½ × 4 × (36 − 16)/5 = 40/5 = 8 N; the remaining KE ½ × 4 × 16 = 32 J is removed in 32/8 = 4 m. Check: v² falls by 20 over 5 m (4 per metre), and 16 is left, so 4 m. Assuming the speed falls equally per metre gives 10 m.

questions.q: A constant force F = (2î + 3ĵ) N acts on a particle while it moves from the point (1, 2) m to the point (4, 6) m. The work done by the force is:
questions.x: Displacement d = (4 − 1)î + (6 − 2)ĵ = 3î + 4ĵ m, so W = F · d = 2 × 3 + 3 × 4 = 18 J. Using the final position vector instead of the displacement gives 26 J; multiplying the magnitudes √13 × 5 assumes F and d are parallel.

questions.q: A uniform disc spins freely on a smooth vertical axle. An identical disc, not spinning, is dropped gently onto it on the same axle, and the two then turn together. What fraction of the original rotational kinetic energy is lost?
questions.x: Angular momentum is conserved: Iω = 2Iω′, so ω′ = ω/2. New KE = ½(2I)(ω/2)² = ¼Iω², half of the original ½Iω², so one half is lost (to friction between the discs). Answering zero confuses conservation of angular momentum with conservation of kinetic energy.

questions.q: Blood leaves the heart through the aorta, of cross-sectional area 4 cm², at an average speed of 30 cm s⁻¹. It then passes through capillaries whose total cross-sectional area is 2400 cm². The average speed of blood in the capillaries is:
questions.x: Continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so v₂ = 4 × 30/2400 = 120/2400 = 0.05 cm s⁻¹. Multiplying by the larger area instead of dividing gives 18000 cm s⁻¹; the others are decimal slips.

questions.q: Several pendulums of different lengths hang from one taut horizontal string. A heavy pendulum 60 cm long hanging from the same string is set swinging. After a while, the pendulum that swings with the largest amplitude is the one:
questions.x: The heavy pendulum drives all the others at its own frequency. The one whose natural frequency matches, the pendulum of the same length (T = 2π√(l/g)), is in resonance and swings most. Bob mass does not set a pendulum's natural frequency.

questions.q: Sound travels at 300 m s⁻¹ in a gas of density 1.5 kg m⁻³ at a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Using Laplace's formula, the ratio of specific heats γ of the gas is:
questions.x: From v = √(γP/ρ), γ = v²ρ/P = 9 × 10⁴ × 1.5/10⁵ = 1.35. Inverting the ratio gives 0.74; 1.16 is √1.35; 1.67 is the value for a monatomic gas, not this one.

questions.q: A ship's sonar sends a sound pulse straight down. The echo from the sea bed returns after 2 s. Sound travels at 1500 m s⁻¹ in sea water. The depth of the sea is:
questions.x: In 2 s the pulse travels 1500 × 2 = 3000 m, down and back up, so the depth is 3000/2 = 1500 m. Forgetting the return trip gives 3000 m.

questions.q: An engineer places a transparent plastic model of a machine part between two crossed polaroids and loads it. Coloured bands appear in the model. This is used to:
o: Measure the speed of light in the plastic
Show where the stress in the part is concentrated
Find the wavelength of the lamp
Make the part transparent to infrared
questions.x: Stressed plastic changes the polarisation of the light passing through it by different amounts in different places, so between crossed polaroids coloured fringes appear. The fringes crowd together where the stress is greatest; this is photoelastic stress analysis.

questions.q: In Michelson's method an eight-sided mirror rotates at 750 rev s⁻¹, and the image is steady when it turns one-eighth of a revolution during the light's round trip. Taking c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, how far away is the distant mirror?
questions.x: Round-trip time t = 1/(8 × 750) = 1/6000 s. The light travels 2d = ct = 3 × 10⁸/6000 = 5 × 10⁴ m, so d = 25 km. Forgetting that the light goes there and back gives 50 km.

questions.q: A gas is taken once round a complete cycle, and the net work done by the gas in the cycle is 300 J. The net heat absorbed by the gas in the cycle is:
questions.x: After a full cycle the gas returns to its starting state, so ΔU = 0. By the first law the net heat absorbed equals the net work done by the gas, 300 J.

questions.q: When a gas is compressed adiabatically, its temperature rises. The reason is that:
o: Heat flows into the gas from the surroundings
The gas does work on its surroundings
No heat leaves, so the work done on the gas all goes into its internal energy
questions.x: In an adiabatic process Q = 0, so the work done on the gas equals the increase in internal energy, and for an ideal gas a larger internal energy means a higher temperature.

questions.q: In a uniform electric field of 500 V m⁻¹, point Q is 4 cm from point P in the direction of the field. The potential difference V_P − V_Q is:
questions.x: V = Ed = 500 × 0.04 = 20 V, and the potential falls along the field direction, so P is higher: V_P − V_Q = +20 V. Leaving 4 cm unconverted gives 2000 V.

questions.q: A metal sphere of radius 10 cm carries a charge of 3 nC. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², what is the electric field at 5 cm from its centre and at 30 cm from its centre?
questions.x: The charge sits on the outer surface and a Gaussian surface inside encloses none, so E = 0 at 5 cm. Outside, the sphere acts as a point charge: E = 9 × 10⁹ × 3 × 10⁻⁹/0.3² = 300 N C⁻¹. Using the radius instead of 30 cm gives 2700 N C⁻¹; forgetting to square gives 90.

questions.q: Wires P and Q have the same cross-sectional area and carry the same current. Metal P has three times as many free electrons per cubic metre as metal Q. The ratio of drift speeds, v(P) : v(Q), is:
questions.x: From I = nAve, with I, A and e the same, v ∝ 1/n. So P's electrons drift at one-third of Q's speed: 1 : 3. Taking v proportional to n gives 3 : 1.

questions.q: The reciprocal of resistance is called conductance. Its SI unit is the:
questions.x: Conductance G = 1/R, so its unit is Ω⁻¹, named the siemens (S). The ohm metre is the unit of resistivity, not of conductance.

questions.q: A horizontal straight wire 0.5 m long has a mass of 20 g. It lies in a horizontal uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T at right angles to the wire. The current needed for the magnetic force to support the wire's weight is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
questions.x: BIL = mg, so I = mg/(BL) = (0.02 × 10)/(0.4 × 0.5) = 0.2/0.2 = 1 A. Taking 20 g as 0.2 kg gives 10 A; leaving out g gives 0.1 A.

questions.q: The force on a straight wire of length L carrying current I in a uniform magnetic field B is F = I(L × B). The direction of this force is always:
o: Perpendicular to both the wire and the field
Halfway between the wire and the field
questions.x: A vector product is perpendicular to both of the vectors multiplied, so F is at right angles to both L and B. It is never along the field or along the wire.

questions.q: A strong magnet dropped down a vertical copper tube falls much more slowly than an unmagnetised piece of iron of the same size. The reason is that:
o: Copper is strongly magnetic and attracts the magnet to its walls
Air resistance is larger for a magnet than for iron
The tube becomes a permanent magnet that repels the magnet
Eddy currents induced in the tube produce a magnetic field that opposes the magnet's motion
questions.x: The falling magnet changes the flux through each ring of the tube, inducing eddy currents. By Lenz's law their field opposes the motion that causes them, giving an upward drag. Copper itself is not attracted by a magnet.

questions.q: Ordinary AC ammeters and voltmeters are calibrated to read the:
o: Average values over a whole cycle
questions.x: AC meters show rms values, the steady DC values that would give the same heating; the 220 V of the mains is an rms value. The average over a whole cycle is zero, so it would be useless.

questions.q: A crystal of quartz conducts heat and refracts light slightly differently along different directions. This property of crystalline solids is called:
questions.x: Because the particles of a crystal are arranged in a regular lattice, the spacing differs along different directions, so properties such as conductivity and refractive index depend on direction: the crystal is anisotropic. Isotropy (the same in all directions) is the property of amorphous solids.

questions.q: Which statement about how an LED, a photodiode used as a light detector and a photovoltaic cell are operated is correct?
o: The LED is reverse biased, the photodiode is forward biased and the photovoltaic cell is reverse biased
The LED is forward biased, the photodiode is reverse biased and the photovoltaic cell needs no bias
questions.x: An LED needs forward bias so that electrons and holes recombine and emit light. A photodiode works in reverse bias, where its small reverse current rises with light intensity. A photovoltaic cell produces its own e.m.f. from light, so it is used without an external bias.

questions.q: A train moves at 30 m s⁻¹ along a straight track. Inside it, a ball is rolled forward at 5 m s⁻¹ relative to the train, and a lamp sends a beam of light forward. An observer on the ground measures the speeds of the ball and of the light as:
o: 35 m s⁻¹ and c + 30 m s⁻¹
25 m s⁻¹ and c − 30 m s⁻¹
questions.x: At everyday speeds velocities add: 30 + 5 = 35 m s⁻¹ for the ball. By the second postulate, light has the same speed c for every inertial observer, whatever the motion of its source. Adding the train's speed to c is the classical mistake.

questions.q: Classical wave theory, which treats radiation energy as continuous, made a prediction about black-body radiation at short (ultraviolet) wavelengths that disagreed with experiment. It predicted that the intensity would:
o: Fall to zero at all wavelengths
Increase without limit as the wavelength gets shorter
Have a peak exactly where experiment shows one
Be the same at every wavelength
questions.x: Classical theory predicted an intensity rising without limit towards short wavelengths (the 'ultraviolet catastrophe'), whereas experiment shows a peak and then a fall. Planck's quantum hypothesis removed this disagreement.

questions.q: Using 1/λ = R_H (1/2² − 1/n²) with R_H = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹, the shortest wavelength in the Balmer series of hydrogen is about:
questions.x: The shortest wavelength (series limit) has n → ∞, so 1/λ = R_H/4 and λ = 4/(1.097 × 10⁷) ≈ 3.65 × 10⁻⁷ m. n = 3 gives the longest line, 6.56 × 10⁻⁷ m; n = 4 gives 4.86 × 10⁻⁷ m; 9.12 × 10⁻⁸ m is the Lyman series limit.

questions.q: Natural uranium contains only about 0.7% of the fissile isotope U-235, the rest being mostly U-238. Many power reactors use enriched uranium, which means uranium in which:
o: The percentage of U-238 has been increased
Extra neutrons have been added to each nucleus
The percentage of U-235 has been increased
The uranium has been turned into plutonium
questions.x: Slow neutrons cause fission mainly in U-235, so raising its share (to a few per cent) makes a chain reaction easier to sustain. Neutrons cannot simply be added to nuclei, and enrichment does not change uranium into another element.

questions.q: A doctor changes from 2 MHz to 8 MHz ultrasound to examine a structure. Compared with the 2 MHz waves, the 8 MHz waves give:
o: Finer detail but less penetration into the body
questions.x: A higher frequency has a shorter wavelength (λ = v/f), so smaller details can be resolved, but it is absorbed more strongly by tissue, so it does not reach as deep. That is why high frequencies are used for shallow organs and lower ones for deep organs.

questions.q: Ethane, C₂H₆, burns completely in oxygen to give CO₂ and H₂O. What volume of oxygen is needed to burn 10 dm³ of ethane, both gases measured at the same temperature and pressure?
questions.x: 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O. For gases at the same T and P, volume ratio = mole ratio, so O₂ = 10 × 7/2 = 35 dm³. Using 7 : 1 instead of 7 : 2 gives 70 dm³, and 20 dm³ is the volume of CO₂ formed.

questions.q: A salt solution is acidified with dilute HCl and then BaCl₂ solution is added. A white precipitate forms that does not dissolve in the acid. The anion present is:
questions.x: BaSO₄ is a white precipitate insoluble in dilute HCl. BaCO₃ would dissolve in the acid with effervescence (and the acid removes carbonate first), while chloride and nitrate give no precipitate with Ba²⁺.

questions.q: A 2 dm³ bulb of nitrogen at 3 atm is connected to a 3 dm³ bulb of oxygen at 2 atm, at the same temperature. After the gases mix, the total pressure is:
questions.x: By Boyle's law each gas spreads into 5 dm³: p(N₂) = 3 × 2/5 = 1.2 atm and p(O₂) = 2 × 3/5 = 1.2 atm. By Dalton's law the total is 2.4 atm. Adding the starting pressures gives 5.0 atm, averaging them gives 2.5 atm, and 1.2 atm is only one partial pressure.

questions.q: Iodine crystals are soft and sublime easily on gentle warming, although the I–I bond inside each molecule is a strong covalent bond. This is because:
o: The I₂ molecules in the crystal are held together only by weak London forces
Iodine forms a covalent network like diamond
The I–I bonds break on gentle warming
questions.x: Iodine is a molecular solid: subliming it separates whole I₂ molecules by overcoming weak London forces, and the covalent I–I bonds stay intact. Confusing breaking intermolecular forces with breaking bonds is the usual slip.

questions.q: In Rutherford's experiment, a very few alpha particles bounced back from the thin gold foil at large angles. This showed that:
o: Most of the atom is empty space
Electrons are spread evenly through the atom
The positive charge and almost all the mass of the atom are packed into a tiny nucleus
The atom has no positive charge
questions.x: Only a tiny, dense, positive centre could repel a heavy, fast alpha particle back. That most particles went straight through shows the atom is mostly empty space, which is a true conclusion but from a different observation.

questions.q: Which element has the highest second ionisation energy?
questions.x: The second electron of sodium must come from the 2p subshell of Na⁺, which has the stable neon configuration close to the nucleus, so it needs far more energy (about 4560 kJ mol⁻¹). For Mg, Al and Si the second electron still comes from the third shell. Choosing Si follows the rule 'IE increases across a period' without noticing the change of shell.

questions.q: The first ionisation energy of aluminium (578 kJ mol⁻¹) is lower than that of magnesium (738 kJ mol⁻¹), although aluminium has the larger nuclear charge. The reason is that:
o: The electron removed from Al is a 3p electron, which is higher in energy and partly shielded by the 3s electrons
Aluminium has a smaller atomic radius than magnesium
The electron removed from Al comes from a full 3s subshell
Aluminium has fewer electrons in its outer shell than magnesium
questions.x: Mg loses a 3s electron, but Al (3s² 3p¹) loses its single 3p electron, which is higher in energy and shielded by the 3s pair, so it is easier to remove. Al does have the smaller radius, but that would raise, not lower, its ionisation energy.

questions.q: Standard enthalpy changes are normally quoted at which temperature?
questions.x: Standard thermochemical data refer to 298 K (25 °C), with substances in their standard states. 273 K is the temperature of gas STP, a common mix-up.

questions.q: A saturated solution of sodium chloride is in contact with undissolved NaCl crystals at constant temperature. Which statement is correct?
o: Dissolving has stopped completely because the solution is saturated
The mass of undissolved crystals keeps decreasing slowly
The concentration of the solution keeps increasing slowly
Crystals keep dissolving and ions keep crystallising at equal rates
questions.x: A saturated solution with excess solid is a physical dynamic equilibrium: NaCl(s) ⇌ Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) goes on in both directions at equal rates, so the amount of solid and the concentration stay constant. 'Dissolving has stopped' is the static view of equilibrium.

questions.q: An indicator HIn ionises in water: HIn (red) ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻ (yellow). What colour does it show in a strongly acidic solution, and why?
o: Yellow, because the high [H⁺] shifts the equilibrium to the right
Red, because the acid removes HIn
Yellow, because H⁺ reacts with In⁻
Red, because the high [H⁺] shifts the equilibrium to the left
questions.x: Adding H⁺, a product of the ionisation, shifts the equilibrium to the left, so un-ionised HIn (red) dominates. In a basic solution OH⁻ removes H⁺ and the equilibrium shifts right to give yellow In⁻. H⁺ reacting with In⁻ does happen, but it forms red HIn, not yellow.

questions.q: An aqueous solution of a non-electrolyte has an osmotic pressure of 2.46 atm at 27 °C. Taking its molality to be equal to its molarity, at what temperature does it freeze? (R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, Kf of water = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹)
questions.x: π = CRT gives C = 2.46/(0.0821 × 300) ≈ 0.10 mol dm⁻³, so m ≈ 0.10 mol kg⁻¹. ΔTf = 1.86 × 0.10 = 0.186 K, so it freezes at −0.186 °C. Using 27 instead of 300 K gives C ≈ 1.11 and the tempting −2.06 °C.

questions.q: Which of these is an emulsion (a liquid dispersed in a liquid)?
questions.x: Milk is liquid fat dispersed in water, an emulsion. Smoke is solid in gas, fog is liquid in gas (an aerosol) and pumice is gas in solid.

questions.q: In which reaction does hydrogen peroxide act as a reducing agent?
questions.x: With chlorine, oxygen in H₂O₂ goes from −1 to 0 (O₂) while Cl goes from 0 to −1, so H₂O₂ is oxidised and acts as the reducing agent. In the other three reactions its oxygen goes from −1 to −2 (water), so there it is the oxidising agent.

questions.q: A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen can be kept at room temperature for years without forming water, although the reaction is strongly exothermic. The best explanation is that:
o: The reaction is endothermic at room temperature
Hydrogen and oxygen molecules never collide at room temperature
The reaction has a high activation energy, so very few collisions are effective at room temperature
The equilibrium lies on the side of hydrogen and oxygen
questions.x: Being exothermic says nothing about speed. The activation energy is high, so almost no colliding molecules have enough energy; a spark supplies it and the mixture explodes. The molecules do collide, and the equilibrium lies far towards water.

questions.q: Sulphur dioxide dissolves in water to form:
questions.x: SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃ (sulphurous acid), with S still +4. H₂SO₄ comes from SO₃, where S is +6.

questions.q: Beryllium has a diagonal relationship with which element, so that both form covalent chlorides and amphoteric oxides?
questions.x: Be (group 2, period 2) and Al (group 13, period 3) lie diagonally, and their ions have similar charge densities: both give covalent chlorides that act as Lewis acids and amphoteric oxides and hydroxides. Magnesium is Be's group neighbour, not its diagonal partner.

questions.q: The basic structural unit present in all silicate minerals is:
questions.x: Every silicate is built from SiO₄⁴⁻ tetrahedra, with silicon at the centre and four oxygen atoms at the corners, linked in different ways by sharing oxygens. SiO₃²⁻ is the repeating unit of chain silicates, not the basic unit.

questions.q: Iron dissolves in dilute nitric acid, but after being dipped in concentrated nitric acid it no longer reacts with dilute acid. This is because concentrated HNO₃:
o: Forms a thin, protective oxide layer on the iron, making it passive
Reduces the iron surface to a more stable form
Deposits a layer of iron(II) nitrate that will not dissolve
Converts the iron into an alloy with nitrogen
questions.x: Concentrated nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent and coats iron (also Al and Cr) with a thin, unreactive oxide film; this is called passivity. Nitrates of iron are soluble in water, so a nitrate layer could not protect the metal.

questions.q: The slow reaction S₂O₈²⁻ + 2I⁻ → 2SO₄²⁻ + I₂ is speeded up by adding a little Fe³⁺ (or Fe²⁺). The best explanation is that:
o: Iron ions provide a solid surface on which the reactants adsorb
Fe³⁺ forms a stable complex with S₂O₈²⁻ that removes it
Fe³⁺ oxidises I⁻ to I₂ and becomes Fe²⁺, which is then oxidised back to Fe³⁺ by S₂O₈²⁻
Iron ions increase the activation energy of the reverse reaction only
questions.x: Two negative ions repel each other, so their direct reaction is slow; iron switches between +3 and +2, so each step is between oppositely charged ions and the iron is regenerated. Dissolved ions do not provide a surface, so the adsorption option describes heterogeneous catalysis, not this case.

questions.q: 2-Methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CH, reacts with chlorine in light by free-radical substitution. How many different monochloro products, C₄H₉Cl, can form?
questions.x: The molecule has two kinds of hydrogen: nine equivalent H on the three CH₃ groups, giving (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Cl, and one H on the central carbon, giving (CH₃)₃CCl. So 2 products. Counting the three CH₃ groups as different gives 4.

questions.q: How many of these compounds show cis–trans isomerism: pent-2-ene, 2-methylbut-2-ene, 1,2-dichloroethene and propene?
questions.x: Pent-2-ene (CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃) and 1,2-dichloroethene (ClCH=CHCl) have two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon, so they show it. 2-Methylbut-2-ene, (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃, has two CH₃ on one carbon and propene has two H on one carbon, so they do not. Counting 2-methylbut-2-ene because it is a but-2-ene gives 3.

questions.q: 2,3-Dimethylbut-2-ene, (CH₃)₂C=C(CH₃)₂, is treated with ozone and the ozonide is decomposed with zinc and water. The product is:
questions.x: Ozonolysis cuts the C=C and puts C=O on each carbon. Each half is (CH₃)₂C=O, so two molecules of propanone form. Propanal would need an H on each double-bond carbon.

questions.q: Which reagents convert benzene into chlorobenzene?
o: Cl₂ in bright sunlight with no catalyst
Cl₂ with anhydrous FeCl₃, in the dark
questions.x: FeCl₃ polarises Cl₂ to give the electrophile for substitution: C₆H₆ + Cl₂ → C₆H₅Cl + HCl. In sunlight without a catalyst chlorine adds by free radicals instead, giving C₆H₆Cl₆.

questions.q: Any Grignard reagent, RMgX, reacts with methanal, HCHO, and the product is hydrolysed with dilute acid. The product is always a:
questions.x: R adds to the carbon of HCHO, giving RCH₂OMgX and then RCH₂OH; the carbinol carbon has two H atoms, so the alcohol is primary. Other aldehydes give secondary alcohols and ketones tertiary; carboxylic acids come from CO₂.

questions.q: A compound C₇H₈O reacts with sodium to give hydrogen, does not dissolve in aqueous NaOH, and gives no colour with neutral FeCl₃ solution. The compound is:
questions.x: Reaction with Na shows an O–H group, so it is not the ether methoxybenzene. The methylphenols are acidic enough to dissolve in NaOH and give a colour with FeCl₃. Phenylmethanol has its –OH on a CH₂ group, so it behaves as an alcohol.

questions.q: When an aldehyde is warmed with Fehling's solution, a red-brown precipitate forms. The precipitate is:
questions.x: The aldehyde reduces the blue Cu²⁺ complex to Cu⁺, which separates as red Cu₂O. CuO is black, and Cu(OH)₂ is blue; silver metal, not copper, is deposited in the Tollens' test.

questions.q: The ester formed when propan-1-ol is heated with ethanoic acid and a little concentrated H₂SO₄ is:
questions.x: The ester is CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃: the alcohol part is named first (propyl) and the acid part second (ethanoate). Swapping the two parts gives ethyl propanoate, a different ester.

questions.q: Methylamine, CH₃NH₂, reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid. The product is:
questions.x: The lone pair on nitrogen accepts H⁺, so the amine acts as a base and forms a salt: CH₃NH₂ + HCl → CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻. Thinking HCl substitutes the NH₂ group (giving chloromethane) treats the amine like an alcohol.

questions.q: In the ¹H NMR spectrum of ethanal, CH₃CHO, the signal of the –CHO proton is split into a:
questions.x: By the n + 1 rule the CHO proton has three H on the neighbouring carbon, so it is split into 3 + 1 = 4 lines. The CH₃ signal is the doublet (one neighbouring H); mixing up which signal is asked about gives that answer.

questions.q: Ozone in the stratosphere is formed naturally when:
o: Lightning makes nitrogen and oxygen combine
CFCs release chlorine atoms that react with O₂
Ultraviolet light splits O₂ molecules into O atoms, which then combine with O₂
Water vapour is split by infrared radiation
questions.x: O₂ + UV → 2O, then O + O₂ → O₃; ozone is also broken down by UV, and the balance gives the ozone layer. Chlorine from CFCs destroys ozone rather than forming it, the common mix-up.

questions.q: What is the product (101)₂ × (11)₂?
questions.x: (101)₂ = 5 and (11)₂ = 3, and 5 × 3 = 15 = (1111)₂. By shifting: 101 + 1010 = 1111, giving the same answer.

questions.q: A bus in a computer is best described as:
o: A program that moves files between folders
A set of parallel lines that carry signals between components
A storage area that keeps data when power is off
A device that converts digital signals to analogue
questions.x: A bus is a group of parallel wires or lines on which signals travel between the CPU, memory and input/output. A device that converts digital to analogue signals is a modem, not a bus.

questions.q: The system bus of a computer is made up of which three buses?
o: Data bus, power bus and memory bus
Address bus, serial bus and input bus
Control bus, cache bus and output bus
Data bus, address bus and control bus
questions.x: The system bus joins the CPU, memory and input/output and consists of the data bus, address bus and control bus. Power, cache, serial and output buses are not the three standard parts.

questions.q: Which of the following is naturally an analogue signal?
o: The bits sent from a keyboard to the computer
The changing voltage from a microphone as a person speaks
The data stored in a byte of RAM
The on/off pulses in a USB cable
questions.x: A microphone produces a voltage that rises and falls smoothly with the sound wave, which is analogue. Keyboard codes, RAM bytes and USB pulses are made of separate 0 and 1 values, so they are digital.

questions.q: Each of the four numbers in a dotted-decimal IPv4 address can have which range of values?
questions.x: Each number is one octet of 8 bits, and 8 bits give values from 0 to 2⁸ − 1 = 255. So 256 or 300 can never appear in an IPv4 address.

questions.q: Which statement describes an analogue signal?
o: It varies smoothly and continuously over a range of values
It has only the two values 0 and 1
It can only be sent through fibre-optic cable
It is made of separate start and stop bits
questions.x: An analogue signal is a continuous wave, like the sound of a voice, that can take any value in a range. A signal with only separate values such as 0 and 1 is digital.

questions.q: A mobile banking PIN has 4 digits, and each digit can be any of 0 to 9. How many different PINs are possible?
questions.x: Each of the 4 places has 10 choices, so 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 10 000 PINs (0000 to 9999). The answer 9 999 forgets that 0000 is also a PIN.

questions.q: Four virtual machines run on one physical server through a hypervisor. The physical server's power supply fails. What happens?
o: The virtual machines keep running on their own
Only the hypervisor stops, not the virtual machines
questions.x: Virtual machines are isolated from each other's software faults, but they all share the same physical hardware, so a hardware failure stops all of them. This is why important systems are spread over several physical servers.

questions.q: Which medical scan uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves, with a computer building detailed pictures of the inside of the body?
questions.x: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) uses magnets and radio waves, and a computer turns the signals into images. A CT scan uses X-rays and ultrasound uses sound waves.

questions.q: A cell holds the value 0.25 and is then formatted as Percentage with 0 decimal places. What does the cell show?
questions.x: Percentage format multiplies the value by 100 for display, so 0.25 shows as 25%; the stored value is still 0.25. 0.25% would mean the value 0.0025.

questions.q: In an Excel column chart, which part shows the scale of numbers (0, 10, 20, …) against which the height of each column is read?
questions.x: The value axis runs up the side of a column chart and carries the number scale, so each column’s height is read against it. The category axis along the bottom names the columns, and the legend only explains the colours of the data series.

questions.q: A direct file stores each record at the address given by key mod 9 (the remainder after dividing the key by 9). Keys 20 and 29 both give address 2. What is this situation called?
questions.x: 20 mod 9 = 2 and 29 mod 9 = 2, so two different keys are sent to the same address; this is a collision, and one record must be placed elsewhere. Redundancy means the same data stored twice, which is not the case here.

questions.q: Two booking clerks try to sell the last seat on a bus at the same moment. Which DBMS function makes sure the seat is sold only once?
questions.x: Concurrency control manages users who change the same data at the same time, so one sale finishes before the other can use the seat. Normalisation is a design method and does not control simultaneous users.

questions.q: Teaches(TeacherID, SubjectID) has the rows (T1, S1), (T1, S2), (T2, S1), (T3, S3). Which relationship between Teacher and Subject do these rows show?
questions.x: T1 teaches two subjects (S1 and S2), and S1 is taught by two teachers (T1 and T2), so both sides are "many". One-to-many from Teacher would need each subject to have only one teacher, which S1 breaks.

questions.q: On a form, a text box has the Control Source `=[Qty]*[Price]`. The user clicks in it and tries to type 500. What happens?
o: Access does not allow it, because the control shows a calculated expression
500 replaces the result and is saved in the table
500 is saved into the Price field
Qty is changed so that the result becomes 500
questions.x: A calculated control is bound to an expression, not a field, so it cannot be edited; Access says the control is bound to the expression. Its value is never written to the table.

questions.q: Which view of an Access table is used to type field names, choose data types and set field properties?
questions.x: Design View shows the table's structure: field names, data types and properties. Datasheet View shows the records in rows and columns for entering data.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%d", 20 - 14 % 4 * 2);
```
questions.x: % and * have higher precedence than - and are done left to right: 14 % 4 = 2, then 2 * 2 = 4, then 20 - 4 = 16. Doing the subtraction first, (20 - 14) % 4 * 2, would give 4.

questions.q: Which format specifier is used in printf to print a single character?
questions.x: %c prints one character. %s prints a whole string, %d an integer and %f a floating-point number.

questions.q: A program has the prototype `float rate(int n, float p);` and a `float` variable `y`. Which statement calls `rate` correctly?
questions.x: A call gives just the values, one for each parameter in the prototype (here two), with no type names. rate(2.5) passes too few arguments, and writing types inside a call is a syntax error.
The argument expressions are worked out before the call: a + 1 = 4 goes to x and a * 2 = 6 goes to y, so x - y = 4 - 6 = -2. Taking them in the other order gives 2.

questions.q: What does the word `void` mean in the prototype `int getnum(void);`?
o: The function can return a value of any type
The function can take any number of arguments
questions.x: void inside the brackets says the parameter list is empty, so getnum is called as getnum(). The return type here is int; a function that returns nothing has void before its name instead.

questions.q:
What happens when this Python program is run?
```
print("begin")
n = int("12x")
print(n * 2)
```
o: Nothing is printed, because it is a syntax error
begin is printed, then the program stops with a runtime error (ValueError)
questions.x: The code is written correctly, so it starts and line 1 prints begin. Line 2 then fails while running because "12x" is not a whole number, giving a ValueError, so line 3 never runs.

questions.q: A test case for a function normally records:
o: the input values and the expected output
only the name of the programmer
the time taken to compile the program
questions.x: A test case states what to enter and what result should come out, so the actual result can be compared with it. Source code and programmer names do not tell a tester whether the function works.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
class Item:
    rate = 5
    def __init__(self, qty):
        self.qty = qty
    def cost(self):
        return self.qty * Item.rate
i = Item(4)
Item.rate = 7
print(i.cost())
```
questions.x: `cost` reads `Item.rate` when it is called, and by then the class attribute has been changed to 7, so 4 × 7 = 28. 20 would use the old rate, as if it had been copied into the object at creation.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
x = 1
while x < 100:
    x = x * 2 + 1
print(x)
```
questions.x: x goes 1 → 3 → 7 → 15 → 31 → 63 → 127. At 63 the test 63 < 100 is still True, so one more pass gives 127, and then the loop stops. 63 is the last value below 100, not the value printed.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
L = [3, 1, 2]
M = sorted(L)
print(L, M)
```
questions.x: `sorted(L)` returns a new sorted list and leaves L unchanged. It is `L.sort()` that changes L in place and returns None.

questions.q: A stack can hold at most 3 values. Starting empty: push 1, push 2, pop, push 3, push 4, push 5. What happens?
o: The last push causes overflow, as the stack already holds 1, 3 and 4
All pushes succeed; the stack holds 1, 3, 4 and 5
questions.x: After push 1, push 2, pop the stack holds 1; push 3 and push 4 fill it to 1, 3, 4. Pushing 5 onto a full stack is overflow. The pop is safe (underflow is popping an empty stack).

questions.q: The values 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80 are inserted, in that order, into an empty binary search tree. When the tree is searched for 60, which nodes are compared, in order?
questions.x: 60 > 50, so go right to 70; 60 < 70, so go left, reaching 60. A BST search follows one path from the root and never visits 30, which is in the left subtree.

questions.q: In a class, 10 students have an average mark of 60 and the other 30 students have an average mark of 80. What is the average mark of the whole class?
questions.x: Total marks = 10 × 60 + 30 × 80 = 600 + 2,400 = 3,000 for 40 students, so the mean is 3,000 / 40 = 75. 70, the average of 60 and 80, ignores that the second group is three times larger.

questions.q: Which part of a business plan estimates the expected sales, costs and profit for the next few years?
questions.x: Financial projections forecast revenue, costs and profit. Market analysis studies the customers and competitors that those forecasts are based on.

questions.q: What does the passage mainly explain?
o: Why goods trains need more powerful engines than lorries
How rubber tyres were improved for use on railways
Why railway lines are always built through tunnels
How the hardness of wheel and rail makes trains efficient but also limits them
questions.x: The second paragraph explains the efficiency of "steel on steel" and the third the "drawback" of the same hardness. Engine power is played down: the secret lies "not so much in the engine's power".

questions.q: According to the passage, why does a lorry lose more energy in rolling than a train?
o: Its wheels touch the road over a patch no larger than a coin
Its engine is much smaller than a locomotive's
It has to stop more often on busy roads
Its tyres keep flattening and springing back as they turn
questions.x: A rubber tyre "flattens slightly ... and springs back", and "That constant squashing and recovering uses up energy". The coin-sized patch describes the steel wheel on the rail, not the lorry.

questions.q: Which of the following is best supported by the reasoning of the passage?
o: A train driver must start braking much earlier than a lorry driver at the same speed
A lorry carrying the same load would use less fuel than the train
A steel train wheel wears out faster than a rubber tyre
A train can climb any slope if its engine is powerful enough
questions.x: Steel on steel gives "little grip", so a train "needs a long distance to stop" and signals must warn drivers "well in advance"; a rubber tyre, which does not slide so easily, can stop sooner. Fuel is the reverse: rail takes "far less fuel for each tonne".

questions.q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "gradients" most nearly means:
o: bends to the left or right
questions.x: Trains cannot climb "steep slopes", so engineers lay tracks along "gentle gradients", that is, gentle slopes. Bends are a different thing: the lines "curve around hills" to avoid steep gradients.

questions.q: The word "however" in the first sentence of the third paragraph shows that the writer is about to:
o: give another example of the same advantage
repeat the main point of the first paragraph
turn from an advantage of steel to a drawback
describe the early history of the railway
questions.x: "However" marks a contrast: after the efficiency of steel on steel, "The same hardness ... brings a drawback", the lack of grip. It does not add another advantage.

questions.q: What does the passage mainly describe?
o: How making a field level helps farmers use water evenly and well
How lasers are used to measure the size of farms
Why oxen have been replaced by tractors on farms
How farmers can store water in the low corners of fields
questions.x: The passage explains the waste on an uneven field, how laser levelling "solves this", and its other "benefits". Water lying in low corners is the problem, not a way of storing it.

questions.q: According to the passage, what happens when water flows across a field that is higher at one end?
o: It collects in the low parts while the high patches stay dry
It spreads evenly but sinks too quickly
It washes soil from the low corners to the high ones
It flows back into the channel
questions.x: "The water races to the low corners and lies there in pools, while the high patches stay dry". It does not spread evenly; even wetting is what levelling achieves.

questions.q: The passage suggests that a farmer who keeps watering an uneven field is likely to:
o: need less fertiliser than a farmer with a level field
harvest the whole crop on a single day
use more water and harvest a crop that ripens unevenly
need to rent a laser-guided tractor every week
questions.x: On an uneven field water must run "far longer than the crop needs", and since an evenly wetted field makes the crop ripen "together", an uneven one will not. Less fertiliser is wrong: on uneven ground it is "washed into the hollows".

questions.q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "plane" most nearly means:
questions.x: "The beam marks a perfectly level plane", a flat surface that the scraper follows. A wood-smoothing tool also shaves, but here the scraper does the shaving; the plane is the level it is guided to.

questions.q: In the last paragraph, the phrase "such equipment" refers to:
o: the wooden board dragged behind oxen
the channels that carry water to the field
the fertiliser spread on the crop
questions.x: The equipment that small farmers cannot buy, and so rent "for a day", is the tractor with the laser-guided scraper. The wooden board was the old, cheap method used "In the past".
